plan.contextChunk: This figure looks straight down the axis of a chair-form cyclohexane ring in two matched models that color-code the two kinds of hydrogen position. On the left is a space-filling model: a compact dark gray core of ring carbons is surrounded by six large red spheres and six large blue spheres packed against one another, the red ones sitting toward the center of the disc and the blue ones fanning outward around the rim, the two colors alternating as the eye travels around the ring. A magenta arrow at the upper left points to a red sphere and is labeled "Axial"; a blue arrow at the top points to a blue sphere and is labeled "Equatorial". On the right the same view appears as a ball-and-stick model, the six dark gray carbons forming a hexagonal outline, with red spheres projecting from alternating carbons and blue spheres held outward from every carbon on thin pale rods. Separating the two positions by color rather than by perspective lets the reader count them directly, establishing that each ring carbon bears exactly one axial and one equatorial hydrogen and that each face carries three of each in alternating order.

left model: six large red spheres (axial hydrogens) packed toward the center of the disc, alternating around the ring
left model: six large blue spheres (equatorial hydrogens) fanning outward around the rim, alternating with the red ones
left model: magenta arrow pointing to a red sphere with label 'Axial'
left model: blue arrow pointing to a blue sphere with label 'Equatorial'
right model: ball-and-stick representation — six dark gray carbon spheres joined by sticks into a hexagonal chair outline
right model: six red spheres on thin pale rods projecting up/down (axial) from alternating carbons
right model: six blue spheres on thin pale rods held outward (equatorial) from every carbon

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Two matched models sit side by side, separated by ~8 world units along +X (space-filling at x≈-4, ball-and-stick at x≈+4), both viewed nearly straight down the chair's average axis. Chair cyclohexane: six carbons at ring radius ~1.5 units with alternating z of ±0.35 (carbons 1,4 displaced most: z=+0.7 and z=-0.7 for the classic chair). Axial hydrogens: radius ~0.5 (space-filling) or at bond length ~1.1 along vertical rods (ball-and-stick), alternating up/down per carbon. Equatorial hydrogens: radius ~2.0–2.3, roughly in the mean ring plane, angled slightly opposite to that carbon's axial direction. Space-filling spheres: carbons ~0.9 radius dark gray #3a3a3a, hydrogens ~0.75 radius; ball-and-stick: carbons ~0.35 radius, hydrogens ~0.28 radius, rods pale gray #c8c8c8 cylinders ~0.06 radius. Colors: axial red #d94f3d, equatorial blue #3d9bd9, 'Axial' label magenta #c2187b, 'Equatorial' label blue #2b7fb8. Labels and arrows sit at the upper left / top of the left model as in the source.
interactionPlan.notes: Implement hydrogen visibility via material opacity fade (animate over ~300 ms) rather than add/remove so both models stay in sync. Clicked-carbon highlight: emissive boost on the carbon plus its two hydrogens; clicking empty space clears. Keep both models in one scene with a shared group rotation so orbiting moves them together; an orthographic-feel top-down start is approximated by the high elevationDeg perspective camera.

authoredContext:
As shown in the figure, each carbon atom in chair cyclohexane has one axial and one equatorial hydrogen. Furthermore, each side of the ring has three axial and three equatorial hydrogens in an alternating arrangement. For example, if the top side of the ring has axial hydrogens on carbons 1, 3, and 5, then it has equatorial hydrogens on carbons 2, 4, and 6. The reverse is true for the bottom side: carbons 1, 3, and 5 have equatorial hydrogens, but carbons 2, 4, and 6 have axial hydrogens (the figure).

Alternating axial and equatorial positions in chair cyclohexane, looking directly down the ring axis. Each carbon atom has one axial and one equatorial position, and each face has alternating axial and equatorial positions.

The space-filling model and ball and stick model of cyclohexane with alternate axial and equatorial positions, represented by red and blue spheres, respectively.

Note that we haven’t used the words cis and trans in this discussion of cyclohexane conformation. Two hydrogens on the same side of the ring are always cis, regardless of whether they’re axial or equatorial and regardless of whether they’re adjacent. Similarly, two hydrogens on opposite sides of the ring are always trans.

The ball-and-stick model is much smaller and lower than the space-filling model instead of comparable size and placement
The callout arrows in the source point to specific axial/equatorial H's on the front of the molecule; here they are tiny and hard to see
evaluation.notes: Both cyclohexane models with correct red-axial/blue-equatorial color coding and rich, working interactions (H-set toggles, demo steps, click-to-highlight), but the top-down camera and unequal model sizes make the chair geometry and side-by-side composition hard to recognize versus the source.
action_items: Lower the camera elevation (near-frontal, ~10-20°) so the chair conformation of both models is clearly visible as in the source
Align the two models horizontally at equal size and vertical position to match the side-by-side composition
Make the Axial/Equatorial labels larger and reposition the callout arrows so they are clearly visible and point to a front-facing axial and equatorial hydrogen
